claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or an interconnected W ligament network in a Cu matrix.
A thin, controlled Ni coating is applied to the W phase before composite consolidation.
The interfacial Ni layer acts as a wetting agent between W and Cu.
The interfacial Ni layer acts as a diffusion barrier between W and Cu.
The Ni coating enhances bonding between the W and Cu phases.
The Ni coating reduces diffusion pathways associated with phase separation.
The Ni coating reduces diffusion pathways associated with interfacial void nucleation.
Reduced diffusion and enhanced interphase bonding maintain W–Cu interfacial integrity during thermal and irradiation stresses.
Ni coating suppresses phase separation and interfacial void formation under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The Ni-coated composite has higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under the stated service conditions.
The Ni-coated composite has a more stable microstructure than the untreated composite under the stated service conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo phase separation under comparable heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites form interfacial voids under comparable heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal performance of untreated W–Cu composites.
The Ni-coating intervention is compatible with current sintering or deposition protocols.
The intervention is expected to operate under heat-transfer loads and irradiation encountered at W plasma-facing material–Cu cooling-component joints.
The magnitude of any thermal-conductivity improvement remains unquantified.
The long-term stability of the Ni coating under cyclic irradiation remains unquantified.
